title: Staying in the Conversation
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer argues that the most overlooked civic and leadership skill right now is staying present in conversation when discomfort arrives. She cites a Pew finding that 53 percent of Americans think their neighbors have bad morals as evidence of distrust rather than mere disagreement, and treats distrust as what blocks cooperation. Tying this to Step Five (Effective Teams) of her Leadership Connection Model, she holds that teams and communities are built when people remain engaged through tension without performing agreement. She points to the oak tree gatherings of women leaders as a model, where people learned to say help me understand rather than telling others why they are wrong. Her invitation is modest: begin with the neighbor or family member and seek connection, not agreement.
points: Distrust, not disagreement, is the real damage; it erodes the capacity to cooperate and make hard choices.
Effective teams are built by staying engaged through discomfort rather than pretending to agree.
The practical phrase shift is help me understand what you mean in place of let me tell you why you are wrong.
Leadership in this moment begins close to home, with connection rather than agreement or resolution.
quotes: When I first read it, I felt grief, not because people disagree, but because that number isn’t pointing to disagreement. It’s pointing to distrust. And distrust is where civic life goes to die.
A team, a community, is built when people remain engaged through discomfort. Not performatively. Not by pretending to agree. But by staying present long enough for something real to emerge.

I think often of the oak tree gatherings that gave birth to The Art of Soulful Leadership. What started as a small circle of women leaders meeting during a fragile time became, over years, a community genuinely capable of holding complexity. They didn’t build that through alignment on every issue. They built it through civic maturity, tolerating tension without collapse, choosing not to dehumanize, learning to say Help me understand what you mean instead of Let me tell you why you’re wrong.

This is the heart of Citizen Leadership in this moment. Not necessarily walking into halls of power. Beginning closer. With the neighbor. With the person across the table. With the family member you’ve been avoiding.

Fragmentation is the greatest threat we face right now. Not because difference is dangerous, but because disconnection makes us brittle. It turns every disagreement into a threat. It makes every tension feel like proof that we is impossible.
